title: Mercy in power
hookLine: the rulers people still speak of warmly are remembered for mercy

lines: A PARENT, A MANAGER, A REFEREE.
WHICH RULERS ARE SPOKEN OF WARMLY?
cards: A parent at bedtime. A shift manager writing next week's schedule. A teacher holding a red pen over a failing paper.
A referee with a whistle. A landlord reading a late-rent text. None of them is a sultan, but each holds a little power over someone else, and chooses every day how to use it.
This path has walked past a lot of rulers this year. Ask which of them people still speak of warmly, and a pattern shows up. It isn't the size of the army.

teach.h: SALAH AL-DIN AND UMAR: THE MERCY IS TOLD.
teach.b: Go back to two names from earlier this year. Salah al-Din, who retook Jerusalem and let its people ransom themselves and leave, instead of putting the city to the sword.
Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, who began his reforms with his own family's wealth. What people still retell is the mercy. Second, the Qur'an puts mercy at the root of leadership.

teach.h: LENIENT, OR THEY WOULD HAVE SCATTERED.
teach.b: After the battle of Uhud, when some of the companions had failed the Prophet, a verse speaks to him, in Pickthall's translation: "It was by the mercy of Allah that thou wast lenient with them (O Muhammad), for if thou hadst been stern and fierce of heart they would have dispersed from round about thee."
The same verse tells him to pardon them, to ask forgiveness for them, and to consult them. Not to punish: to keep them close and keep listening. Third, a hadith brings this into every household.

teach.h: EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet, peace be upon him, says each of you is a shepherd, responsible for the flock: the ruler for his people, a man for his family, a woman for her husband's household, a servant for what his master left in his care.
Fourth, a hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi: the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful.

teach.h: IT WAS BY THE MERCY OF ALLAH.
teach.b: Be merciful to those on earth, and the One above will be merciful to you. The red pen, the schedule, the whistle: each one a small throne. And the history suggests what will be remembered from it.

how: Muslims often cite the hadith that each person is a shepherd responsible for a flock, and the Qur'an's praise of the Prophet's leniency, when speaking about how parents, employers and leaders should treat those in their care.

the power to forgive the taxes of the poor
a ruler's right to punish as he sees fit

the shepherd hadith is only about rulers

games.q: you lead a community. at a critical moment some of your people left their posts, and it cost dearly. now they're back in front of you. what do you do?
o: make an example of them, so it never happens again.
pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and keep consulting them.
forgive them quietly, but stop asking their advice.
games.why: Qur'an 3:159, after Uhud, praises the Prophet's leniency and tells him to pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the affair.

practice: Ask yourself where you hold a little power over someone, a child, an employee, a student, a person waiting on your reply, and picture the next moment you'll have a choice about them: a mistake to correct, a request to answer, a deadline to enforce.
Don't drop the standard; just see what a lenient answer would look like, the kind that keeps them close.

wordCard.voice: Mercy in power. Leniency and pardon from the one who could punish, the thing people remember of their rulers. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy is remembered. Leniency is what keeps people close. Until tomorrow.
